"You look for the assumption that makes a problem slow, or makes extra compute buy only more of the same. Ask which part
of the work waits on another part, and whether it must. Ask which quantity is measured, and whether a different but
related quantity would be cheaper to compute, easier to split, or more informative. Ask whether the unit of work is the
right one, or whether the work could be cut, merged or reordered. Ask whether the objective is the right one: the single
best answer, a ranking, a distribution, a rare tail, or a yes or no. Ask what is held fixed that need not be. Prefer
changes that alter what more compute buys over changes that only run the same work more times.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: generative pipeline for discovery of single phase immersion coolants
Problem:
**IC-V1 · Force-field error floor for coolant MD: an enlarged C10–C50 benchmark scored against measurement.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · PASS

**Question.** Will graphics-card molecular simulations using Green–Kubo on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters rank immersion coolants' viscosity and thermal conductivity the same way measurements do?

**What is known.** Ogbomo and colleagues, in 2026, used Green–Kubo molecular dynamics to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity for eight C10–C50 molecules at 40 °C and compared with measurements [s_ogbomo_md]. Whether the error is a correctable bias or a random floor that caps ranking, and how rank agreement holds over hundreds of molecules [s_ogbomo_db].

**Hypothesis.** Green–Kubo MD with one fixed force field has a chemistry-dependent error floor near 25 percent that more molecules cannot remove [s_ogbomo_res].

**If compute is the lever.** At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent and rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 [s_ogbomo_res].

**If not.** Held-out viscosity error stays above 25 percent and rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size, capping candidate ranking [s_ogbomo_res].

**Test.** One LAMMPS LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo protocol at 40 °C, six five-nanosecond replicas per molecule, run on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules from the public 835-molecule reference set, scored only against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity [s_ogbomo_db].

*Compute axis.* Benchmark molecules scored against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity: 8–120 molecules, 4 levels. Closest prior: 8 [s_ogbomo_md], beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Repeat the published eight-molecule Green–Kubo run first: density within 4% for seven molecules and thermal conductivity over-predicted for all eight [s_ogbomo_res]. Tolerance: same bias signs for viscosity and thermal conductivity; density error within 4 percentage points of the published error; per-molecule viscosity within 20% of the reference value.

**Would not show.** Shows transport-property error only at 40 °C for pure liquids between 1 and 50 mPa·s, not blends or sold coolants. Cannot show ranking behaviour beyond 120 molecules.

*Cost.* Plans $940.98 of the $1,000 budget over 59 machine-hours, leaving $59.02. Main guess: assumed MD throughput per GPU [p], measured after $36.20 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.1× lower. 3 cost flags in the block.

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

The task: analyze the research problem about Green-Kubo MD force-field error floor for coolant viscosity/thermal conductivity ranking. Find where compute stops helping (the hypothesis says error floor ~25% caps ranking; more molecules don't help). Reframings: changes to what is measured, unit of work, objective, or order of steps. Up to three reframes, each ending with a specific question, cheapest measurement, cost estimate, and fields per schema.

Key insight: The bottleneck is force-field systematic error (chemistry-dependent bias), not sampling. More replicas/molecules only buy more of the same bias. So reframes should target:

1. Change the measured quantity: instead of absolute transport properties scored against measurement, measure differences/ratios (e.g., relative viscosity between molecules at same conditions, or trends vs carbon number) — errors may cancel in relative quantities. Or measure a cheaper proxy quantity that correlates: e.g., enthalpy of vaporization, density, cohesive energy density, self-diffusion (cheaper via Einstein relation than Green-Kubo), or dielectric? Actually for ranking, the quantity could be rank-ordering of a proxy like diffusion coefficient (cheaper to converge than viscosity/thermal conductivity via Green-Kubo). Einstein-relation diffusion converges much faster than Green-Kubo viscosity. So: measure self-diffusion as a screening proxy; check if D ranks the same as measured viscosity (Stokes-Einstein-ish inverse relation). Cheapest measurement: compute D for ~20 molecules with short trajectories, compare rank with measured viscosity — maybe $50.

2. Change the unit of work: instead of per-molecule independent runs, use molecule pairs/differences — alchemical or direct comparison; or restructure to bias-correction learning: fit per-chemistry-class correction (group contribution) — compute buys correction parameters. Actually the plan already includes bias correction. Alternative: reframe unit of work from "molecule" to "error mode": cluster molecules by functional group, and use compute to identify transferable correction per class. Or reorder: instead of benchmark-then-trust, do active/adaptive sampling — spend compute only on molecules that change ranking decisions (boundary between candidate classes). Objective change: from "rank all molecules" to "answer yes/no: is molecule X better than the incumbent coolant?" — pairwise comparison with error cancellation; compute buys decision confidence, not global rank. Question: does paired-difference MD (same force field, matched protocols) rank pairs correctly more often than absolute prediction? Cheapest measure: pick 10 pairs with known measured viscosity order, run paired simulations, count sign agreement of Δη.

3. Change objective from transport properties to a tail/decision: screen for rare candidates in tail (low viscosity AND high thermal conductivity) — classification at decision threshold rather than full ranking. Or change what is held fixed: force field fixed → allow per-class re-parameterization or use compute to fit a correction from experimental data (machine-learned delta correction). Question: can a two-parameter per-class correction fit on 30 molecules with measurements reduce held-out error below 15%? Cheapest measure: fit on existing 8-molecule published data + new 12-molecule runs, evaluate on holdout — cost estimate.

Also: change what's measured — measure viscosity via a different method (NEMD, reverse NEMD, transient-time correlation function) that converges faster; the assumption that Green-Kubo is the right estimator. Compute then buys longer averaging where it matters. But the bottleneck is force-field error, not estimator noise — so estimator change only helps if estimator biases interact.

Let me structure three reframes:

Reframe 1 (change measured quantity → relative/pairwise differences): 
- Bottleneck: force-field systematic error floor ~25% caps absolute accuracy; more molecules/replicas buy the same bias.
- Assumption: the quantity scored must be absolute viscosity/thermal conductivity per molecule.
- Reframe: score pairwise differences (Δη, Δλ between molecule pairs) computed with identical protocol; systematic errors partially cancel in differences; compute then buys correct ordering decisions rather than absolute accuracy.
- Question: "Does the sign of the simulated viscosity difference agree with the sign of the measured viscosity difference for molecule pairs whose measured viscosities differ by more than 15%?"
- Measure: 20 pairs spanning the measured viscosity range (1–50 mPa·s), 2×5 ns each; count sign agreement and rank correlation of differences. Cost: ~40 short MD runs ≈ maybe $60–120. Let's say ≈$80, a few GPU-days.
- compute_after: more compute buys more pairs / finer decision boundaries near ties, improving decision accuracy where it matters, not re-measuring the same bias.
- exact: sign agreement measured as fraction of pairs where sign(Δη_sim) = sign(Δη_meas), with per-pair Δ from paired Green-Kubo runs.
- expected: sign agreement ≥0.85 for pairs separated by ≥15% measured difference even though absolute error stays ~25%.
- fails_if: sign agreement ≤0.6 for well-separated pairs — bias is molecule-specific and random, not systematic; pairwise cancellation fails.
- closest_prior: Ogbomo 8-molecule single-property comparison [s_ogbomo_md]; no paired-difference analysis.

Reframe 2 (change unit of work / estimator → cheaper proxy, diffusion-based screening):
- Bottleneck: Green-Kubo viscosity and thermal conductivity converge slowly; most of the $940 spend buys statistical averaging of a quantity whose accuracy is capped by the force field, so extra compute buys only more of the same bias at high precision.
- Assumption: the screening quantity must be the transport coefficient itself via Green-Kubo.
- Reframe: use self-diffusion (Einstein relation, converges ~10–50× faster) plus density/cohesive energy as a cheap proxy screen; reserve expensive Green-Kubo for top candidates. Test whether proxy ranks track measured viscosity ranks.
- Question: "Does the rank correlation between simulated self-diffusion coefficient and measured viscosity exceed 0.8 across 40 molecules spanning the reference set?"
- Measure: 40 molecules, one 2-ns replica each for D and density; Spearman correlation vs measured viscosity. Cost: ~$40–80 (2 ns × 40). Say ≈$50.
- compute_after: compute buys funnel depth — cheap proxy on all 835 molecules, expensive GK only on survivors; each dollar moves the decision set rather than repeating bias.
- exact: Spearman ρ between D_sim (Einstein MSD slope) and measured η at 40 °C over 40 molecules.
- expected: |ρ| ≥ 0.8 (inverse relation), justifying two-stage funnel.
- fails_if: |ρ| < 0.5 — proxy not informative; screening cannot be delegated.
- closest_prior: Ogbomo used GK only on 8 molecules [s_ogbomo_md]; no proxy validation in [s_ogbomo_db].

Reframe 3 (change objective / what held fixed → per-chemistry-class transferable correction, objective as classification at decision threshold):
- Bottleneck: hypothesis says chemistry-dependent error floor; plan treats error as scalar bias to subtract after the fact, and tests at fixed set sizes — compute beyond ~48 molecules only re-measures the floor.
- Assumption: force field held fixed, and the objective is global rank agreement over the whole benchmark.
- Reframe: (a) objective → yes/no: "is candidate X better than the single-phase incumbent on both properties?" — a two-class decision needing only local accuracy near the decision boundary; (b) hold fixed less: allow a small per-class (alkane vs ester, per carbon-number slope) correction model learned jointly with the benchmark, with compute allocated adaptively to molecules nearest the decision boundary (active learning).
- Question: "Can a class-conditional linear correction (slope per chemistry class vs carbon number) fit on ≤30 molecules reduce held-out viscosity error below 15% and push decision accuracy (better/worse than incumbent) above 90%?"
- Measure: fit correction on 30 molecules with known measurements (reusing published 8 + 22 new runs), evaluate error and decision accuracy on 20 held-out. Cost: ~22 new molecules × 6 replicas × 5 ns ≈ $170; reuse keeps under ~$200. Say ≈$180.
- compute_after: additional compute buys boundary resolution — molecules near the decision threshold get more replicas; more compute changes which side of the line candidates fall on, not just confidence in a capped rank.
- exact: held-out MAPE for viscosity after class-conditional correction; decision accuracy = fraction of held-out molecules correctly classified better/worse than incumbent on both η and λ.
- expected: held-out error <15%, decision accuracy ≥0.9 at 50 molecules total.
- fails_if: residual error stays >25% with no class structure (correction R² < 0.3) — error is irreducible per-molecule noise; reframe dead.
- closest_prior: [s_ogbomo_res] bias-correction plan as scalar; class-conditional correction not in prior.

Ordering steps reframe could be merged into #3 (adaptive allocation). Good.

Costs should be consistent with the $1,000 budget, $940 plan, 59 machine-hours → ~$16/hr. 6 replicas × 5 ns = 30 ns per molecule. If plan: 8+24+48+120 = 200 molecule-protocols... actually cumulative levels. Cost ~$940 for 200 molecules × 30 ns = 6000 ns → ~$0.16/ns → ~59 machine-hours → 6000 ns / 59 hr ≈ 100 ns per machine-hour? That seems fast but fine. So per-molecule cost ≈ 940/200 ≈ $4.70. Hmm, then 40 molecules × 2 ns = 80 ns ≈ $13. Let me just keep rough estimates: reframe 1: 40 runs × 5 ns = 200 ns ≈ $32; say ≈$30–40. Reframe 2: 40 × 2 ns = 80 ns ≈ $15. Reframe 3: 22 new × 30 ns = 660 ns ≈ $105. Use these scaled numbers.

Let me finalize: reframe 1 ≈ $35, reframe 2 ≈ $15, reframe 3 ≈ $110.

Return only JSON matching schema: array "reframes" with objects containing all required keys.

Compute then buys correct ordering decisions rather than absolute accuracy.","question":"For molecule pairs whose measured viscosities differ by at least 15%, what fraction have sign(Δη_simulated) = sign(Δη_measured) when both legs use the same LOPLS-AA Green-Kubo protocol?","measure":"20 molecule pairs spanning 1–50 mPa·s from the reference set, 2 replicas × 5 ns per leg (200 ns total), count sign agreement of simulated vs measured viscosity differences. Rough cost $35 (about 2 machine-hours at the plan's throughput), done before scaling further.","compute_after":"More compute adds pairs and resolves near-tie pairs with extra replicas, directly improving decision accuracy at ranking boundaries instead of re-measuring a fixed bias.","exact":"Sign agreement = fraction of the 20 pairs where the simulated viscosity difference has the same sign as the measured difference, with per-leg η from the standard Green-Kubo integral at 40 °C.","expected":"Sign agreement ≥ 0.85 for pairs separated by ≥15% measured difference, even while absolute per-molecule error remains ~25%, showing the floor is largely common-mode.","fails_if":"Sign agreement ≤ 0.6 on well-separated pairs, meaning the error is molecule-specific noise rather than shared systematic bias, so differencing buys nothing.","closest_prior":"Ogbomo's 8-molecule study compared absolute simulated vs measured values only [s_ogbomo_md]; — and unfix the field minimally by learning a class-conditional correction (per chemistry class, linear in carbon number) jointly with the benchmark, with compute allocated adaptively to molecules nearest the decision boundary.","question":"Can a class-conditional linear correction fit on 30 molecules with known measurements reduce held-out viscosity error below 15% and raise better/worse-than-incumbent decision accuracy above 90% on 20 held-out molecules?","measure":"Run 22 new molecules (reusing the published 8 for the fit set) at 6 replicas × 5 ns (~660 ns), fit per-class slope/intercept corrections on 30, evaluate held-out MAPE and decision accuracy on 20. Rough cost $110 (about 7 machine-hours).","compute_after":"Further compute buys boundary resolution: extra replicas and extra molecules are spent only where the classification is uncertain, so more compute moves candidates across the decision line instead of shrinking error bars on a capped global rank.","exact":"Held-out viscosity MAPE after applying the class-conditional correction, and decision accuracy = fraction of 20 held-out molecules correctly classified as better or worse than the incumbent on both η and λ.","expected":"Held-out error < 15% and decision accuracy ≥ 0.9 with the correction explaining most of the chemistry-dependent bias (correction R² > 0.7).","fails_if":"Residual held-out error stays above 25% with correction R² < 0.3, i.e., no class structure to the bias, meaning the error is irreducible per-molecule noise and neither correction nor boundary-focused compute can help.","closest_prior":"The plan's own bias-correction step treats error as a single scalar [s_ogbomo_res]; no class-conditional or decision-threshold framing appears in [s_ogbomo_md] or [s_ogbomo_db]."}]}
